items.bodyEn: Shirasuka once stood by the shore below the hill. The great Hōei earthquake of 1707 sent a tsunami through it, and the whole post town was rebuilt on the top of Shiomizaka, the 'tide-viewing slope'. From there travelers bound for Edo got their first wide view of the Pacific; Hiroshige painted a daimyō's procession winding down toward that sea.
items.sourceNote: Shirasuka post-town records (1707 Hōei quake relocation); Hiroshige 'Shirasuka'

items.bodyEn: Hiroshige titled his print 汐見阪, but today the hill is written 潮見坂. Both 潮 and 汐 read しお and mean tide: 潮 pairs water with 朝 (morning), 汐 pairs it with 夕 (evening) — the morning and evening tides of old Chinese usage. Modern Japanese keeps 潮 for everything (潮風, 満潮, 風潮) and leaves 汐 to names and poetry.
items.sourceNote: Standard kanji dictionaries (新字源): 潮 = 氵+朝 morning tide, 汐 = 氵+夕 evening tide

items.bodyEn: 諦める now means 'to give up', yet it began as 明らめる, 'to make clear'. The kanji 諦 is Buddhist: the 四諦 are the Four Noble Truths, the things seen as they truly are. Seeing a situation plainly and accepting it slid into letting it go. The old sense survives in written 諦観, clear-eyed acceptance rather than defeat.
items.sourceNote: Kōjien / Nihon Kokugo Daijiten, entry あきらめる (明らめる); Buddhist term 四諦

items.bodyEn: 〜ずにはいられない is literally 'cannot stay without doing': the written ず from Arai, plus に, plus はいられない. It names an urge you cannot hold back — 笑わずにはいられない, I can't help laughing. 〜ないわけにはいかない looks similar but means duty: 行かないわけにはいかない, I have no choice but to go. Remember する → せずにはいられない.
items.ja: {笑|わら}わずにはいられない。
items.kana: わらわずにはいられない。
